children = | relatives = | religion = | origin = Japan | nationality = Japanese }} {{Nihongo|'''Momotarō'''|桃太郎||"Peach Boy"}} is a {{ill|Folk hero|en|Folk hero|WD=Q84164296|lt=popular hero}} of [[Japanese folklore]]. His name is often translated as ''Peach Boy'', but is directly translated as ''{{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=Peach}} + {{ill|Tarō (given name)|en|Tarō (given name)|WD=Q2293011|lt=Tarō}}'', a common Japanese given name. ''Momotarō'' is also the title of various books, films and other works that portray the tale of this hero. There is a popular notion that Momotarō is a local hero of {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}, but this claim was invented in the modern era. This notion is not accepted as consensus in scholarly circles. ==Story== [[File:Japanese Fairy Book - Ozaki - 247.png|thumb|Momotarō coming out of a peach]] The present conventional form of the tale (Standard Type) can be summarized as follows:{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=163–164}}{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}
Momotarō was born from a giant peach, which was found floating down a river by an old, childless woman who was washing clothes there. The woman and her husband discovered the child when they tried to open the peach to eat it. The child explained that he had been bestowed by the gods to be their son. The couple named him Momotarō, from ''momo'' (peach) and ''tarō'' (eldest son in the family). When he was just five years old, he was able to cut a big tree with just an old knife. When he matured into adolescence, Momotarō left his parents to fight a band of ''{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}'' (demons or ogres) who marauded over their land, by seeking them out in the distant island where they dwelled (a place called Onigashima or "Demon Island"). En route, Momotarō met and befriended a talking {{ill|Dog|en|Dog|WD=Q144|lt=Dog}}, {{ill|Monkey|en|Monkey|WD=Q1367|lt=Monkey}} and {{ill|Pheasant|en|Pheasant|WD=Q214169|lt=Pheasant}}, who agreed to help him in his quest in exchange for a portion of his rations (''{{ill|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|en|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|WD=Q18383509|lt=kibi dango}}'' or "millet dumplings"). At the island, Momotarō and his animal friends penetrated the demons' fort and beat the band of demons into surrendering. Momotarō and his new friends returned home with the demons' plundered treasure and the demon chief as a captive.
This Standard Type of "Momotarō" was defined and popularized due to them being printed in school textbooks during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji Period}}.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}: This is the result of development of the literary "Momotarō", which had been handwritten and printed since the early {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} into Meiji.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} One significant change is that in most examples of Edo Period literature, Momotarō was not born from a peach, but born naturally to the elderly couple who ate the peach and regained their youth. Such subtypes are classed as {{nihongo||回春型|kaishun-gata|extra2="rejuvenation" type}}, whereas the now conventional subtypes are termed {{nihongo||果生型|kasei-gata|extra2="birth from the fruit" type}}.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} ==Development in literature== Although the oral version of the story may have emerged during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1392–1573), it may not have been set down in writing until the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1603–1867).{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} The oldest works of Momotaro known to have existed had been dated to the {{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku}} era (1688–1704) or perhaps earlier.{{sfnp|Tierney|2005|p=143}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} ===Edo period=== These older texts from around the Genroku era (e.g. ''Momotarō mukashigatari'') are lost,{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} but surviving examples of later dates, such as the reprint ''Saihan Momotarō mukashigatari'' (c. 1777{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|An undated copy exists, but is probably nearly coeval with a second copy dated [[An'ei]]6 or 1777.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|pp=51–53}}}}) purportedly preserve the older tradition, and form the first (most primitive) group of texts according to {{interlanguage link|Koike Tōgorō|ja|小池藤五郎}}.{{harvp|Koike|1967|pp=23, 28ff}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24ff}}, the first (''dai-ichi keitō'') group of texts. The late date of the reprint has sometimes caused it to be classed as ''{{ill|Kibyōshi|en|Kibyōshi|WD=Q3196335|lt=Kibyōshi}}'' ("yellow cover" book, directed primarily at an adult audience) or later type of ''{{ill|Kusazōshi|en|Kusazōshi|WD=Q862334|lt=Kusazōshi}}'' literature (intended for a more general audience, including women and children), but it should properly be classed as ''{{ill|akahon|en|akahon|WD=Q4700148|lt=akahon}}'' ("red book") or early type.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=53}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The original print must have been produced in the ''akahon'' era. The reprint bears the illustrator's name "Nishimura Shigenobu" which was the name this artist used early in his career, from {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 16/1731 to c. [[Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyō]] 4/1747.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=52}}{{r|ukiyoejiten}}}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Kumooka's paper also calls it an ''akahon''{{sfnp|Kumooka|2016|p=34ff}}}} A second group of texts, which Koike considered to be younger, includes the miniature ''akahon'', {{nihongo||『もゝ太郎』|Momotarō}}, printed in {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 8 (1723).{{Efn|The title uses the Japanese [[ditto mark]] "ゝ".}}{{harvp|Koike|1972}}, pp. 19ff. 24ff/ This miniature book is now considered to be the oldest surviving copy of any written Momotarō story.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=57}} Whether belonging to the first or second groups, texts from the Edo Period generally follow the same general plot as the modern standard versions but exhibit certain differences in detail. ====Dumpling, kindling, animals==== Momotarō is not supplied with ''kibi dango'' ("millet dumplings"), but rather with {{nihongo||[[:ja:十団子|とう団子]]|tō dango}} and other treats in the oldest Genroku era texts and the first group.{{harvp|Koike|1967|p=21}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|p=26}} In the first group, the old man goes out to cut grass, rather than to cut {{linktext|kindling}}. The same three companion beasts (pheasant, monkey, then dog) appear in both groups, but in a different order.{{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24–28}} (comparison chart). Though the order of the animals is not significant to the story, the most common order that appear is the dog, the monkey, and then the pheasant. In nearly every variation, all three animal companions agree to help Momotarō in exchange for a portion of his food. In one variation from the Edo Period, the dog is given half a portion, the monkey willingly comes, and Momotarō threatens the pheasant. ====Birth from peach==== As noted above, in most of the Edo Period books, peach boy is not born from a peach but from the woman who consumes a peach and grows years younger in age. Both the first and second groups consist entirely of "rejuvenation" types. The "birth from the peach" type examples (such as the version in {{ill|Takizawa Bakin|en|Takizawa Bakin|WD=Q463142|lt=Takizawa Bakin}}'s 1811 essay {{interlanguage link|Enseki zasshi{{!}}''Enseki zasshi''|ja|燕石雑志|}} "Swallowstone Miscellany") are found among tales that have deviated further, which Koike assigns to a third group of texts. While "birth from the peach" version has not been confirmed in earlier written texts from the Edo Period, one tantalizing sculpture dating to 1614 depicted a man standing in the middle of a split peach. This purported Momotarō carving at [[Kehi Jingū|Kehi Shrine]] in {{ill|Tsuruga, Fukui|en|Tsuruga, Fukui|WD=Q847581|lt=Tsuruga, Fukui}} was lost during the air raids of 1945.{{Efn|Koike thought it looked like an old man riding a peach like a boat, and that it could not be conclusively connected to Momotarō.}}{{sfnp|Koike|1967|pp=36–37}} ====Momotarō's age==== [[File:Momotarō ehon.jpg|thumb|right|360px|Momotaro swinging the magic mallet ({{ill|Uchide no kozuchi|en|Uchide no kozuchi|WD=Q7876713|lt=Uchide no kozuchi}}), with his animal companions.{{right|{{small|―Santō-an Kyōden ({{ill|Santō Kyōden|en|Santō Kyōden|WD=Q938347|lt=Santō Kyōden}}). ''Ehon takara no nanakusa'' (1804)}}}}]] It was noted that the protagonist Momotarō was being drawn progressively younger by artists over the years. In one subjective estimation, Momotarō appeared about age 30-ish until c. 1735, 25-ish up to c. 1800, and 20-ish until the end of Edo Period in 1867.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}} Not every text specifies age, but in the version in {{nihongo|Kamo no Norikiyo|賀茂規清}} (1798–1861)'s {{nihongo|''Hina no Ukegi''|雛迺宇計木}} Momotarō's was 15 years and 6 months when he set out on his expedition.{{sfnp|Koike|1957|p=9}}{{Efn|[[East Asian age reckoning]] applies, so it really means June in the year he turned or will turn 15.}} And in ''Momotarō takara no kurairi'' (c. 1830–40), Momotarō was aged sixteen.{{cite book|author=Ifuku Sanjin |others=Utagawa Hiroshige, illustr. |script-title=ja:桃太郎宝蔵入 |title=Momotarō takara no kurairi |publisher=Sanoya |date=1830–1840|language=ja}}{{cite web|title=Momotaro and the Ogres' Treasure House |work=Edo Picture Books and Japanisme |publisher=National Diet Library |year=2018 |url=https://www.kodomo.go.jp/gallery/edoehon/momotarou/index_e.html |access-date=2019-04-26}} The Momotarō in Iwaya Sazanami's version of 1894 was of similar age (15 years old) when he resolved to go to devil island.{{harvp|Ozaki|1903|p=249}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1904|p=6}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|p=6}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Momotarō illustrated in this work appeared 18 or 19 years old to Koike.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}}}} Researcher {{interlanguage link|Namekawa Michio|ja|滑川道夫}} also noticed the trend of Momotarō being depicted younger and younger, and he dubbed the phenomenon {{Nihongo|"tendency of age diminishment"|低年齢化傾向|teinenreika keikō}}.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=99}}{{r|ito}} ===Meiji period=== After Japan abandoned the feudal system and entered the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, {{interlanguage link|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} became a seminal figure in how the Momotaro story was shaped and became familiarized to the Japanese populace. Sazanami was the author of the Momotaro tales in his commercially successful folktale collections, and also a major contributor to the textbook versions. The "Momotarō" tale was first incorporated into nationalized textbooks for [[:en:Elementary schools|Elementary schools]] by the Meiji government in 1887.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{Refn|{{harvp|Torigoe|1983|p=3}}, cited by Hori in English.}}{{harvp|Namekawa|1981|p=ii}}, cited by {{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}} in English. It was subsequently omitted from the 1st edition of the National Language Reader or {{interlanguage link|Kokugo tokuhon{{!}}''Kokugo tokuhon''|ja|国語読本}} but reappeared from the 2nd edition onward to the 5th edition.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}} It has been generally accepted that the 2nd edition reader of 1910 was ''de facto'' written by storybook author Iwaya Sazanami, who had joined the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|en|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|WD=Q11080185|lt=Ministry of Education}} as nonpermanent staff in 1906.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}{{r|rogala}} Iwaya had already published a version of "Momotaro" (1894) for his ''Nihon mukashibanashi'' ([[:en:Japanese Folktales|Japanese Folktales]]), where Momotaro is cast as a military soldier or commander ({{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}) of Great Japan (Dainihon), dispatched on a punitive campaign to quell the ogres who live in the northeast.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=47}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=66|}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}} Older texts took the punishing of ''oni'' for granted and dispensed with explaining what crimes the oni committed to deserve condemnation. But in Iwaya's version, the ogres were explicitly stated as being evil beings, who devoured the "poor people" and taken "plunder" from the Emperor's land of Japan ({{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Ozaki}}'s translation{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=250}}), thus morally justifying Momotaro's expedition.{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}}{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=28–29}} It has been suggested these ogres represented the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}} of China since the publication occurred in 1895, which saw the outbreak of the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=Sino-Japanese War}}.{{harvp|Tierney|2005|pp=118, 263}} ===Taishō and Shōwa eras=== From the 3rd edition National Language Reader (1918–1932) onwards (until the end of {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}), "Momotaro" has occupied the spot of the last tale in Book 1 of these nationalized elementary textbook series.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}} Teachers in essays submitted in 1917 stated that the perception of the Momotaro tale was shifting, so that they were seen as containing lessons of assertiveness and helping in the material advancement of one's country.{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Maruyama (1917), p. 17 and Kinoshita (1917), p. 127 There was criticism from the {{ill|Liberalism|en|Liberalism|WD=Q6216|lt=Liberalism}} side, for example, the novelist [[:en:Yuzo Yamamoto|Yamamoto Yūzō]] (1925) protesting that the ''oni'' were being punished for no apparent reason, and is "tantamount to telling [children] to think of foreigners as ''oni''".{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Yamamoto (1977), collected works, vol. 10, pp. 288ff In the early {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}, after Emperor {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Hirohito}} assumed the throne, Momotarō continued to be used to instill patriotism (or the teachings of the [[Imperial Rescript on Education|Rescript on Education]]) pupils with the 4th edition National Language Reader (1933–1938) which begins with the picture of the cherry blossom.{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=161–162, 179}} The "Momotarō" of the 4th edition was modified so that the ''oni'' now stated "We will no longer torment the people nor take things. Please spare our lives", and forfeits their treasures out of their own volition, thus addressing the foregoing issues (i.e., Momotarō accused of attacking ''oni'' for no legitimate reason).{{harvp|Kahara|2010|pp=51}} and English abstract. The use of Momotarō in wartime propaganda against the U.S. and its Allies was discussed extensively by {{ill|John W. Dower|en|John W. Dower|WD=Q903632|lt=John W. Dower}} in his book ''{{ill|War Without Mercy|en|War Without Mercy|WD=Q55637403|lt=War Without Mercy}}'' (1986). Dower is credited with coining the term "Momotarō paradigm" in this respect.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|pp=}}{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=165–167}} Momotarō disappeared from Japanese textbooks at the end of World War II.{{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}}, note 4. ==Oral variants== The story has some regional variations in oral telling. In some variants, a red and white box are seen floating down the river, and when the red box is chosen to be recovered, Momotarō is found inside. These may be a red box and a black box, or the box may contain a peach inside. These types are often seen in the northern parts of Japan ([[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] and {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku}} regions).{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Seki|1978|pp=81–83}} Or Momotarō may exhibit the characteristic of the lazy protagonist in the {{interlanguage link|Sannen Netarō{{!}}''Netarō''|ja|三年寝太郎}} "Sleeping Boy" stories. These subtypes have been collected mainly in the [[Shikoku]] and {{ill|Chūgoku region|en|Chūgoku region|WD=Q127864|lt=Chūgoku}} regions.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=40}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=334}} There are variances about the Momotarō's process of growth; one is that he grew up to meet the expectation of the old couple to be a fine boy. Another is that he grew up to be a strong but lazy person who just sleeps all day and does not do anything. It is possible that the Momotarō being a fine boy version is more famous to give lessons to children. Nowadays, Momotarō is one of the most famous characters in Japan, as an ideal model for young kids for his kind-heartedness, bravery, power, and care for his parents. Grown up, Momotarō goes on his journey to defeat the demons when he hears about the demons of the Onigashima (demon island). In some versions of the story, Momotarō volunteered to go help the people by repelling the demons, but in some stories he was forced by the townspeople or others to go on a journey. However, all the stories describe Momotarō defeating the Oni and living 'happily ever after' with the old couple. ==Claims as local hero== Momotarō now enjoys popular association with {{ill|Okayama|en|Okayama|WD=Q200078|lt=Okayama}} City or its prefecture, but this association was only created in the modern era.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|pp=51, 61}}, and passim. The publication of a book by Nanba Kinnosuke entitled ''Momotarō no Shijitsu'' (1930) for example helped the notion of Momotarō's origins in Okayama to gain wider familiarity.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|pp=44–47}} Still, even as late as the antebellum period before {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}} (1941–1945), Okayama was considered only the third contender behind two other regions known as Momotarō's homeland.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=51}} The demon island ({{Nihongo|Onigashima|鬼ヶ島}}) of the story is sometimes associated with {{ill|Megijima|en|Megijima|WD=Q339004|lt=Megijima}} Island, an island in the [[Seto Inland Sea]] near {{ill|Takamatsu|en|Takamatsu|WD=Q200707|lt=Takamatsu}}, due to the vast manmade caves found there.{{cite web |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080110004627/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-date=2008-01-10 |title=Oni-ga-shima(or Megijima) |access-date=2010-09-01}}{{Cite web |title=Megi-jima/Ogi-jima |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |website=Takamatsu City Web Site |access-date=2010-09-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100731105152/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |archive-date=2010-07-31 |url-status=dead }} {{ill|Inuyama, Aichi|en|Inuyama, Aichi|WD=Q503411|lt=Inuyama, Aichi}} has {{interlanguage link|Momotarō Shrine (Inuyama)|ja|桃太郎神社 (犬山市)|lt=Momotarō Shrine}} with a legend associated with it.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=42, 461}} In the 1920s and 1930s, lyricist {{ill|Ujō Noguchi|en|Ujō Noguchi|WD=Q2748367|lt=Ujō Noguchi}} wrote three "folk songs" for the locality alluding to the Momotaro legend.{{efn|{{nihongo|《犬山音頭》《桃太郎音頭》《犬山節》|"Inuyama ondo", "Momotarō ondo", "Inuyama bushi"}}.}} ==English translations== [[File:Momotaro-Kobunsha-1885-insidecover.jpg|thumb|English ''Momotaro'' published by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s Kōbunsha (1885, 1st edition)]] The story has been translated into English many times. "The Adventures of Little Peachling" appeared in [[:en:A.B. Mitford|A.B. Mitford]]'s ''{{ill|Tales of Old Japan|en|Tales of Old Japan|WD=Q7679344|lt=Tales of Old Japan}}'' in 1871. {{ill|William Elliot Griffis|en|William Elliot Griffis|WD=Q2066943|lt=William Elliot Griffis}} published a version in 1880, which remained obscure even to researchers, even though English translations in subsequent decades apparently borrowed from Griffis's phraseology and use of idiom, sometimes even copying outright.{{sfnp|Griffis|1880|pp=62–71}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Rev. David Thompson's translation as "Little Peachling" appeared as the first volume of {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s ''Japanese Fairy Tale'' series in 1885. A second edition appeared in 1886, with a different set of illustrations, drawn by {{ill|Kobayashi Eitaku|en|Kobayashi Eitaku|WD=Q2784105|lt=Kobayashi Eitaku}} Susan Ballard included the tale in ''Fairy Tales from Far Japan'' (1899). {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki}} included a loosely translated version in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903); Ozaki's retellings were based on a version by "Sadanami sanjin" (''sic.'', i.e., {{interlanguage link|Sazanami Iwaya|ja|巌谷小波}}).{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''nom de plume'' of Sazanami Iwaya".{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Ozaki was credited with spreading Japanese folktales to the English-speaking nations by researchers such as {{interlanguage link|Teiji Seta|ja|瀬田貞二}}.{{Efn|Seta is well-known as the Japanese translator of [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] novels.}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} There was another English translation that used the same source as Ozaki and published around the same time, namely, "The Story of Peach-Boy" in ''Iwaya's Fairy Tales of Old Japan'' (1903, repub. 1914) translated by {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell}}.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The bilingual 1903 edition was published by Eigaku-shimpo-sha, in 12 volumes. In 1914, the English translations were bound together as "12 parts in 1 vol".}} The translation of the collection was a collaborative effort with other translators, such as Fanny B. Greene, {{ill|Tsuda Umeko|en|Tsuda Umeko|WD=Q514524|lt=Tsuda Umeko}} and others. This latter effort was acknowledged by Iwaya himself.{{harvp|Iwaya|1904}}, foreword.{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=240}} Teresa Peirce Williston in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'', Second Series, in 1911. The tale was translated as ''Peach-Prince and the Demons'' and included in the compilation ''Fairy stories my children love best of all'', although the compiler did not indicate its Japanese origin.Shimer, Edgar Dubs. ''Fairy stories my children love best of all''. New York: L. A. Noble. 1920. pp. 73-79. children = | relatives = | religion = | origin = Japan | nationality = Japanese }} {{Nihongo|'''Momotarō'''|桃太郎||"Peach Boy"}} is a {{ill|Folk hero|en|Folk hero|WD=Q84164296|lt=popular hero}} of [[Japanese folklore]]. His name is often translated as ''Peach Boy'', but is directly translated as ''{{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=Peach}} + {{ill|Tarō (given name)|en|Tarō (given name)|WD=Q2293011|lt=Tarō}}'', a common Japanese given name. ''Momotarō'' is also the title of various books, films and other works that portray the tale of this hero. There is a popular notion that Momotarō is a local hero of {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}, but this claim was invented in the modern era. This notion is not accepted as consensus in scholarly circles. ==Story== [[File:Japanese Fairy Book - Ozaki - 247.png|thumb|Momotarō coming out of a peach]] The present conventional form of the tale (Standard Type) can be summarized as follows:{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=163–164}}{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}
Momotarō was born from a giant peach, which was found floating down a river by an old, childless woman who was washing clothes there. The woman and her husband discovered the child when they tried to open the peach to eat it. The child explained that he had been bestowed by the gods to be their son. The couple named him Momotarō, from ''momo'' (peach) and ''tarō'' (eldest son in the family). When he was just five years old, he was able to cut a big tree with just an old knife. When he matured into adolescence, Momotarō left his parents to fight a band of ''{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}'' (demons or ogres) who marauded over their land, by seeking them out in the distant island where they dwelled (a place called Onigashima or "Demon Island"). En route, Momotarō met and befriended a talking {{ill|Dog|en|Dog|WD=Q144|lt=Dog}}, {{ill|Monkey|en|Monkey|WD=Q1367|lt=Monkey}} and {{ill|Pheasant|en|Pheasant|WD=Q214169|lt=Pheasant}}, who agreed to help him in his quest in exchange for a portion of his rations (''{{ill|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|en|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|WD=Q18383509|lt=kibi dango}}'' or "millet dumplings"). At the island, Momotarō and his animal friends penetrated the demons' fort and beat the band of demons into surrendering. Momotarō and his new friends returned home with the demons' plundered treasure and the demon chief as a captive.
This Standard Type of "Momotarō" was defined and popularized due to them being printed in school textbooks during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji Period}}.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}: This is the result of development of the literary "Momotarō", which had been handwritten and printed since the early {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} into Meiji.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} One significant change is that in most examples of Edo Period literature, Momotarō was not born from a peach, but born naturally to the elderly couple who ate the peach and regained their youth. Such subtypes are classed as {{nihongo||回春型|kaishun-gata|extra2="rejuvenation" type}}, whereas the now conventional subtypes are termed {{nihongo||果生型|kasei-gata|extra2="birth from the fruit" type}}.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} ==Development in literature== Although the oral version of the story may have emerged during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1392–1573), it may not have been set down in writing until the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1603–1867).{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} The oldest works of Momotaro known to have existed had been dated to the {{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku}} era (1688–1704) or perhaps earlier.{{sfnp|Tierney|2005|p=143}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} ===Edo period=== These older texts from around the Genroku era (e.g. ''Momotarō mukashigatari'') are lost,{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} but surviving examples of later dates, such as the reprint ''Saihan Momotarō mukashigatari'' (c. 1777{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|An undated copy exists, but is probably nearly coeval with a second copy dated [[An'ei]]6 or 1777.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|pp=51–53}}}}) purportedly preserve the older tradition, and form the first (most primitive) group of texts according to {{interlanguage link|Koike Tōgorō|ja|小池藤五郎}}.{{harvp|Koike|1967|pp=23, 28ff}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24ff}}, the first (''dai-ichi keitō'') group of texts. The late date of the reprint has sometimes caused it to be classed as ''{{ill|Kibyōshi|en|Kibyōshi|WD=Q3196335|lt=Kibyōshi}}'' ("yellow cover" book, directed primarily at an adult audience) or later type of ''{{ill|Kusazōshi|en|Kusazōshi|WD=Q862334|lt=Kusazōshi}}'' literature (intended for a more general audience, including women and children), but it should properly be classed as ''{{ill|akahon|en|akahon|WD=Q4700148|lt=akahon}}'' ("red book") or early type.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=53}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The original print must have been produced in the ''akahon'' era. The reprint bears the illustrator's name "Nishimura Shigenobu" which was the name this artist used early in his career, from {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 16/1731 to c. [[Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyō]] 4/1747.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=52}}{{r|ukiyoejiten}}}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Kumooka's paper also calls it an ''akahon''{{sfnp|Kumooka|2016|p=34ff}}}} A second group of texts, which Koike considered to be younger, includes the miniature ''akahon'', {{nihongo||『もゝ太郎』|Momotarō}}, printed in {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 8 (1723).{{Efn|The title uses the Japanese [[ditto mark]] "ゝ".}}{{harvp|Koike|1972}}, pp. 19ff. 24ff/ This miniature book is now considered to be the oldest surviving copy of any written Momotarō story.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=57}} Whether belonging to the first or second groups, texts from the Edo Period generally follow the same general plot as the modern standard versions but exhibit certain differences in detail. ====Dumpling, kindling, animals==== Momotarō is not supplied with ''kibi dango'' ("millet dumplings"), but rather with {{nihongo||[[:ja:十団子|とう団子]]|tō dango}} and other treats in the oldest Genroku era texts and the first group.{{harvp|Koike|1967|p=21}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|p=26}} In the first group, the old man goes out to cut grass, rather than to cut {{linktext|kindling}}. The same three companion beasts (pheasant, monkey, then dog) appear in both groups, but in a different order.{{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24–28}} (comparison chart). Though the order of the animals is not significant to the story, the most common order that appear is the dog, the monkey, and then the pheasant. In nearly every variation, all three animal companions agree to help Momotarō in exchange for a portion of his food. In one variation from the Edo Period, the dog is given half a portion, the monkey willingly comes, and Momotarō threatens the pheasant. ====Birth from peach==== As noted above, in most of the Edo Period books, peach boy is not born from a peach but from the woman who consumes a peach and grows years younger in age. Both the first and second groups consist entirely of "rejuvenation" types. The "birth from the peach" type examples (such as the version in {{ill|Takizawa Bakin|en|Takizawa Bakin|WD=Q463142|lt=Takizawa Bakin}}'s 1811 essay {{interlanguage link|Enseki zasshi{{!}}''Enseki zasshi''|ja|燕石雑志|}} "Swallowstone Miscellany") are found among tales that have deviated further, which Koike assigns to a third group of texts. While "birth from the peach" version has not been confirmed in earlier written texts from the Edo Period, one tantalizing sculpture dating to 1614 depicted a man standing in the middle of a split peach. This purported Momotarō carving at [[Kehi Jingū|Kehi Shrine]] in {{ill|Tsuruga, Fukui|en|Tsuruga, Fukui|WD=Q847581|lt=Tsuruga, Fukui}} was lost during the air raids of 1945.{{Efn|Koike thought it looked like an old man riding a peach like a boat, and that it could not be conclusively connected to Momotarō.}}{{sfnp|Koike|1967|pp=36–37}} ====Momotarō's age==== [[File:Momotarō ehon.jpg|thumb|right|360px|Momotaro swinging the magic mallet ({{ill|Uchide no kozuchi|en|Uchide no kozuchi|WD=Q7876713|lt=Uchide no kozuchi}}), with his animal companions.{{right|{{small|―Santō-an Kyōden ({{ill|Santō Kyōden|en|Santō Kyōden|WD=Q938347|lt=Santō Kyōden}}). ''Ehon takara no nanakusa'' (1804)}}}}]] It was noted that the protagonist Momotarō was being drawn progressively younger by artists over the years. In one subjective estimation, Momotarō appeared about age 30-ish until c. 1735, 25-ish up to c. 1800, and 20-ish until the end of Edo Period in 1867.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}} Not every text specifies age, but in the version in {{nihongo|Kamo no Norikiyo|賀茂規清}} (1798–1861)'s {{nihongo|''Hina no Ukegi''|雛迺宇計木}} Momotarō's was 15 years and 6 months when he set out on his expedition.{{sfnp|Koike|1957|p=9}}{{Efn|[[East Asian age reckoning]] applies, so it really means June in the year he turned or will turn 15.}} And in ''Momotarō takara no kurairi'' (c. 1830–40), Momotarō was aged sixteen.{{cite book|author=Ifuku Sanjin |others=Utagawa Hiroshige, illustr. |script-title=ja:桃太郎宝蔵入 |title=Momotarō takara no kurairi |publisher=Sanoya |date=1830–1840|language=ja}}{{cite web|title=Momotaro and the Ogres' Treasure House |work=Edo Picture Books and Japanisme |publisher=National Diet Library |year=2018 |url=https://www.kodomo.go.jp/gallery/edoehon/momotarou/index_e.html |access-date=2019-04-26}} The Momotarō in Iwaya Sazanami's version of 1894 was of similar age (15 years old) when he resolved to go to devil island.{{harvp|Ozaki|1903|p=249}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1904|p=6}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|p=6}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Momotarō illustrated in this work appeared 18 or 19 years old to Koike.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}}}} Researcher {{interlanguage link|Namekawa Michio|ja|滑川道夫}} also noticed the trend of Momotarō being depicted younger and younger, and he dubbed the phenomenon {{Nihongo|"tendency of age diminishment"|低年齢化傾向|teinenreika keikō}}.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=99}}{{r|ito}} ===Meiji period=== After Japan abandoned the feudal system and entered the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, {{interlanguage link|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} became a seminal figure in how the Momotaro story was shaped and became familiarized to the Japanese populace. Sazanami was the author of the Momotaro tales in his commercially successful folktale collections, and also a major contributor to the textbook versions. The "Momotarō" tale was first incorporated into nationalized textbooks for [[:en:Elementary schools|Elementary schools]] by the Meiji government in 1887.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{Refn|{{harvp|Torigoe|1983|p=3}}, cited by Hori in English.}}{{harvp|Namekawa|1981|p=ii}}, cited by {{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}} in English. It was subsequently omitted from the 1st edition of the National Language Reader or {{interlanguage link|Kokugo tokuhon{{!}}''Kokugo tokuhon''|ja|国語読本}} but reappeared from the 2nd edition onward to the 5th edition.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}} It has been generally accepted that the 2nd edition reader of 1910 was ''de facto'' written by storybook author Iwaya Sazanami, who had joined the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|en|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|WD=Q11080185|lt=Ministry of Education}} as nonpermanent staff in 1906.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}{{r|rogala}} Iwaya had already published a version of "Momotaro" (1894) for his ''Nihon mukashibanashi'' ([[:en:Japanese Folktales|Japanese Folktales]]), where Momotaro is cast as a military soldier or commander ({{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}) of Great Japan (Dainihon), dispatched on a punitive campaign to quell the ogres who live in the northeast.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=47}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=66|}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}} Older texts took the punishing of ''oni'' for granted and dispensed with explaining what crimes the oni committed to deserve condemnation. But in Iwaya's version, the ogres were explicitly stated as being evil beings, who devoured the "poor people" and taken "plunder" from the Emperor's land of Japan ({{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Ozaki}}'s translation{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=250}}), thus morally justifying Momotaro's expedition.{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}}{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=28–29}} It has been suggested these ogres represented the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}} of China since the publication occurred in 1895, which saw the outbreak of the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=Sino-Japanese War}}.{{harvp|Tierney|2005|pp=118, 263}} ===Taishō and Shōwa eras=== From the 3rd edition National Language Reader (1918–1932) onwards (until the end of {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}), "Momotaro" has occupied the spot of the last tale in Book 1 of these nationalized elementary textbook series.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}} Teachers in essays submitted in 1917 stated that the perception of the Momotaro tale was shifting, so that they were seen as containing lessons of assertiveness and helping in the material advancement of one's country.{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Maruyama (1917), p. 17 and Kinoshita (1917), p. 127 There was criticism from the {{ill|Liberalism|en|Liberalism|WD=Q6216|lt=Liberalism}} side, for example, the novelist [[:en:Yuzo Yamamoto|Yamamoto Yūzō]] (1925) protesting that the ''oni'' were being punished for no apparent reason, and is "tantamount to telling [children] to think of foreigners as ''oni''".{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Yamamoto (1977), collected works, vol. 10, pp. 288ff In the early {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}, after Emperor {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Hirohito}} assumed the throne, Momotarō continued to be used to instill patriotism (or the teachings of the [[Imperial Rescript on Education|Rescript on Education]]) pupils with the 4th edition National Language Reader (1933–1938) which begins with the picture of the cherry blossom.{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=161–162, 179}} The "Momotarō" of the 4th edition was modified so that the ''oni'' now stated "We will no longer torment the people nor take things. Please spare our lives", and forfeits their treasures out of their own volition, thus addressing the foregoing issues (i.e., Momotarō accused of attacking ''oni'' for no legitimate reason).{{harvp|Kahara|2010|pp=51}} and English abstract. The use of Momotarō in wartime propaganda against the U.S. and its Allies was discussed extensively by {{ill|John W. Dower|en|John W. Dower|WD=Q903632|lt=John W. Dower}} in his book ''{{ill|War Without Mercy|en|War Without Mercy|WD=Q55637403|lt=War Without Mercy}}'' (1986). Dower is credited with coining the term "Momotarō paradigm" in this respect.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|pp=}}{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=165–167}} Momotarō disappeared from Japanese textbooks at the end of World War II.{{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}}, note 4. ==Oral variants== The story has some regional variations in oral telling. In some variants, a red and white box are seen floating down the river, and when the red box is chosen to be recovered, Momotarō is found inside. These may be a red box and a black box, or the box may contain a peach inside. These types are often seen in the northern parts of Japan ([[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] and {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku}} regions).{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Seki|1978|pp=81–83}} Or Momotarō may exhibit the characteristic of the lazy protagonist in the {{interlanguage link|Sannen Netarō{{!}}''Netarō''|ja|三年寝太郎}} "Sleeping Boy" stories. These subtypes have been collected mainly in the [[Shikoku]] and {{ill|Chūgoku region|en|Chūgoku region|WD=Q127864|lt=Chūgoku}} regions.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=40}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=334}} There are variances about the Momotarō's process of growth; one is that he grew up to meet the expectation of the old couple to be a fine boy. Another is that he grew up to be a strong but lazy person who just sleeps all day and does not do anything. It is possible that the Momotarō being a fine boy version is more famous to give lessons to children. Nowadays, Momotarō is one of the most famous characters in Japan, as an ideal model for young kids for his kind-heartedness, bravery, power, and care for his parents. Grown up, Momotarō goes on his journey to defeat the demons when he hears about the demons of the Onigashima (demon island). In some versions of the story, Momotarō volunteered to go help the people by repelling the demons, but in some stories he was forced by the townspeople or others to go on a journey. However, all the stories describe Momotarō defeating the Oni and living 'happily ever after' with the old couple. ==Claims as local hero== Momotarō now enjoys popular association with {{ill|Okayama|en|Okayama|WD=Q200078|lt=Okayama}} City or its prefecture, but this association was only created in the modern era.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|pp=51, 61}}, and passim. The publication of a book by Nanba Kinnosuke entitled ''Momotarō no Shijitsu'' (1930) for example helped the notion of Momotarō's origins in Okayama to gain wider familiarity.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|pp=44–47}} Still, even as late as the antebellum period before {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}} (1941–1945), Okayama was considered only the third contender behind two other regions known as Momotarō's homeland.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=51}} The demon island ({{Nihongo|Onigashima|鬼ヶ島}}) of the story is sometimes associated with {{ill|Megijima|en|Megijima|WD=Q339004|lt=Megijima}} Island, an island in the [[Seto Inland Sea]] near {{ill|Takamatsu|en|Takamatsu|WD=Q200707|lt=Takamatsu}}, due to the vast manmade caves found there.{{cite web |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080110004627/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-date=2008-01-10 |title=Oni-ga-shima(or Megijima) |access-date=2010-09-01}}{{Cite web |title=Megi-jima/Ogi-jima |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |website=Takamatsu City Web Site |access-date=2010-09-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100731105152/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |archive-date=2010-07-31 |url-status=dead }} {{ill|Inuyama, Aichi|en|Inuyama, Aichi|WD=Q503411|lt=Inuyama, Aichi}} has {{interlanguage link|Momotarō Shrine (Inuyama)|ja|桃太郎神社 (犬山市)|lt=Momotarō Shrine}} with a legend associated with it.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=42, 461}} In the 1920s and 1930s, lyricist {{ill|Ujō Noguchi|en|Ujō Noguchi|WD=Q2748367|lt=Ujō Noguchi}} wrote three "folk songs" for the locality alluding to the Momotaro legend.{{efn|{{nihongo|《犬山音頭》《桃太郎音頭》《犬山節》|"Inuyama ondo", "Momotarō ondo", "Inuyama bushi"}}.}} ==English translations== [[File:Momotaro-Kobunsha-1885-insidecover.jpg|thumb|English ''Momotaro'' published by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s Kōbunsha (1885, 1st edition)]] The story has been translated into English many times. "The Adventures of Little Peachling" appeared in [[:en:A.B. Mitford|A.B. Mitford]]'s ''{{ill|Tales of Old Japan|en|Tales of Old Japan|WD=Q7679344|lt=Tales of Old Japan}}'' in 1871. {{ill|William Elliot Griffis|en|William Elliot Griffis|WD=Q2066943|lt=William Elliot Griffis}} published a version in 1880, which remained obscure even to researchers, even though English translations in subsequent decades apparently borrowed from Griffis's phraseology and use of idiom, sometimes even copying outright.{{sfnp|Griffis|1880|pp=62–71}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Rev. David Thompson's translation as "Little Peachling" appeared as the first volume of {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s ''Japanese Fairy Tale'' series in 1885. A second edition appeared in 1886, with a different set of illustrations, drawn by {{ill|Kobayashi Eitaku|en|Kobayashi Eitaku|WD=Q2784105|lt=Kobayashi Eitaku}} Susan Ballard included the tale in ''Fairy Tales from Far Japan'' (1899). {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki}} included a loosely translated version in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903); Ozaki's retellings were based on a version by "Sadanami sanjin" (''sic.'', i.e., {{interlanguage link|Sazanami Iwaya|ja|巌谷小波}}).{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''nom de plume'' of Sazanami Iwaya".{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Ozaki was credited with spreading Japanese folktales to the English-speaking nations by researchers such as {{interlanguage link|Teiji Seta|ja|瀬田貞二}}.{{Efn|Seta is well-known as the Japanese translator of [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] novels.}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} There was another English translation that used the same source as Ozaki and published around the same time, namely, "The Story of Peach-Boy" in ''Iwaya's Fairy Tales of Old Japan'' (1903, repub. 1914) translated by {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell}}.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The bilingual 1903 edition was published by Eigaku-shimpo-sha, in 12 volumes. In 1914, the English translations were bound together as "12 parts in 1 vol".}} The translation of the collection was a collaborative effort with other translators, such as Fanny B. Greene, {{ill|Tsuda Umeko|en|Tsuda Umeko|WD=Q514524|lt=Tsuda Umeko}} and others. This latter effort was acknowledged by Iwaya himself.{{harvp|Iwaya|1904}}, foreword.{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=240}} Teresa Peirce Williston in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'', Second Series, in 1911. The tale was translated as ''Peach-Prince and the Demons'' and included in the compilation ''Fairy stories my children love best of all'', although the compiler did not indicate its Japanese origin.Shimer, Edgar Dubs. Momotarō. | first_major = | first_minor = | first_date = | first = | last_major = | last_minor = | last_date = | last = | creator = | based_on = | adapted_by = | designer = | portrayer = | voice = | motion_actor = | full_name = | nickname = | alias = | species = | gender = Male | title = | occupation = | affiliation = | fighting_style = | weapon = | family = | spouse = | significant_other = | children = | relatives = | religion = | origin = Japan | nationality = Japanese }} {{Nihongo|'''Momotarō'''|桃太郎||"Peach Boy"}} is a {{ill|Folk hero|en|Folk hero|WD=Q84164296|lt=popular hero}} of [[Japanese folklore]]. His name is often translated as ''Peach Boy'', but is directly translated as ''{{ill|Peach|en|Peach|WD=Q13189|lt=Peach}} + {{ill|Tarō (given name)|en|Tarō (given name)|WD=Q2293011|lt=Tarō}}'', a common Japanese given name. ''Momotarō'' is also the title of various books, films and other works that portray the tale of this hero. There is a popular notion that Momotarō is a local hero of {{ill|Okayama Prefecture|en|Okayama Prefecture|WD=Q132936|lt=Okayama Prefecture}}, but this claim was invented in the modern era. This notion is not accepted as consensus in scholarly circles. ==Story== [[File:Japanese Fairy Book - Ozaki - 247.png|thumb|Momotarō coming out of a peach]] The present conventional form of the tale (Standard Type) can be summarized as follows:{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=163–164}}{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}
Momotarō was born from a giant peach, which was found floating down a river by an old, childless woman who was washing clothes there. The woman and her husband discovered the child when they tried to open the peach to eat it. The child explained that he had been bestowed by the gods to be their son. The couple named him Momotarō, from ''momo'' (peach) and ''tarō'' (eldest son in the family). When he was just five years old, he was able to cut a big tree with just an old knife. When he matured into adolescence, Momotarō left his parents to fight a band of ''{{ill|Oni|en|Oni|WD=Q730052|lt=Oni}}'' (demons or ogres) who marauded over their land, by seeking them out in the distant island where they dwelled (a place called Onigashima or "Demon Island"). En route, Momotarō met and befriended a talking {{ill|Dog|en|Dog|WD=Q144|lt=Dog}}, {{ill|Monkey|en|Monkey|WD=Q1367|lt=Monkey}} and {{ill|Pheasant|en|Pheasant|WD=Q214169|lt=Pheasant}}, who agreed to help him in his quest in exchange for a portion of his rations (''{{ill|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|en|Kibi dango (millet dumpling)|WD=Q18383509|lt=kibi dango}}'' or "millet dumplings"). At the island, Momotarō and his animal friends penetrated the demons' fort and beat the band of demons into surrendering. Momotarō and his new friends returned home with the demons' plundered treasure and the demon chief as a captive.
This Standard Type of "Momotarō" was defined and popularized due to them being printed in school textbooks during the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji Period}}.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=39}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}: This is the result of development of the literary "Momotarō", which had been handwritten and printed since the early {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} into Meiji.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} One significant change is that in most examples of Edo Period literature, Momotarō was not born from a peach, but born naturally to the elderly couple who ate the peach and regained their youth. Such subtypes are classed as {{nihongo||回春型|kaishun-gata|extra2="rejuvenation" type}}, whereas the now conventional subtypes are termed {{nihongo||果生型|kasei-gata|extra2="birth from the fruit" type}}.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} ==Development in literature== Although the oral version of the story may have emerged during the {{ill|Muromachi period|en|Muromachi period|WD=Q334845|lt=Muromachi period}} (1392–1573), it may not have been set down in writing until the {{ill|Edo period|en|Edo period|WD=Q184963|lt=Edo period}} (1603–1867).{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=39}} The oldest works of Momotaro known to have existed had been dated to the {{ill|Genroku|en|Genroku|WD=Q1325001|lt=Genroku}} era (1688–1704) or perhaps earlier.{{sfnp|Tierney|2005|p=143}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} ===Edo period=== These older texts from around the Genroku era (e.g. ''Momotarō mukashigatari'') are lost,{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=25}} but surviving examples of later dates, such as the reprint ''Saihan Momotarō mukashigatari'' (c. 1777{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|An undated copy exists, but is probably nearly coeval with a second copy dated [[An'ei]]6 or 1777.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|pp=51–53}}}}) purportedly preserve the older tradition, and form the first (most primitive) group of texts according to {{interlanguage link|Koike Tōgorō|ja|小池藤五郎}}.{{harvp|Koike|1967|pp=23, 28ff}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24ff}}, the first (''dai-ichi keitō'') group of texts. The late date of the reprint has sometimes caused it to be classed as ''{{ill|Kibyōshi|en|Kibyōshi|WD=Q3196335|lt=Kibyōshi}}'' ("yellow cover" book, directed primarily at an adult audience) or later type of ''{{ill|Kusazōshi|en|Kusazōshi|WD=Q862334|lt=Kusazōshi}}'' literature (intended for a more general audience, including women and children), but it should properly be classed as ''{{ill|akahon|en|akahon|WD=Q4700148|lt=akahon}}'' ("red book") or early type.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=53}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The original print must have been produced in the ''akahon'' era. The reprint bears the illustrator's name "Nishimura Shigenobu" which was the name this artist used early in his career, from {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 16/1731 to c. [[Enkyō (Edo period)|Enkyō]] 4/1747.{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=52}}{{r|ukiyoejiten}}}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|Kumooka's paper also calls it an ''akahon''{{sfnp|Kumooka|2016|p=34ff}}}} A second group of texts, which Koike considered to be younger, includes the miniature ''akahon'', {{nihongo||『もゝ太郎』|Momotarō}}, printed in {{ill|Kyōhō|en|Kyōhō|WD=Q1145048|lt=Kyōhō}} 8 (1723).{{Efn|The title uses the Japanese [[ditto mark]] "ゝ".}}{{harvp|Koike|1972}}, pp. 19ff. 24ff/ This miniature book is now considered to be the oldest surviving copy of any written Momotarō story.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Yamasaki|2018|p=57}} Whether belonging to the first or second groups, texts from the Edo Period generally follow the same general plot as the modern standard versions but exhibit certain differences in detail. ====Dumpling, kindling, animals==== Momotarō is not supplied with ''kibi dango'' ("millet dumplings"), but rather with {{nihongo||[[:ja:十団子|とう団子]]|tō dango}} and other treats in the oldest Genroku era texts and the first group.{{harvp|Koike|1967|p=21}}, {{harvp|Koike|1972|p=26}} In the first group, the old man goes out to cut grass, rather than to cut {{linktext|kindling}}. The same three companion beasts (pheasant, monkey, then dog) appear in both groups, but in a different order.{{harvp|Koike|1972|pp=24–28}} (comparison chart). Though the order of the animals is not significant to the story, the most common order that appear is the dog, the monkey, and then the pheasant. In nearly every variation, all three animal companions agree to help Momotarō in exchange for a portion of his food. In one variation from the Edo Period, the dog is given half a portion, the monkey willingly comes, and Momotarō threatens the pheasant. ====Birth from peach==== As noted above, in most of the Edo Period books, peach boy is not born from a peach but from the woman who consumes a peach and grows years younger in age. Both the first and second groups consist entirely of "rejuvenation" types. The "birth from the peach" type examples (such as the version in {{ill|Takizawa Bakin|en|Takizawa Bakin|WD=Q463142|lt=Takizawa Bakin}}'s 1811 essay {{interlanguage link|Enseki zasshi{{!}}''Enseki zasshi''|ja|燕石雑志|}} "Swallowstone Miscellany") are found among tales that have deviated further, which Koike assigns to a third group of texts. While "birth from the peach" version has not been confirmed in earlier written texts from the Edo Period, one tantalizing sculpture dating to 1614 depicted a man standing in the middle of a split peach. This purported Momotarō carving at [[Kehi Jingū|Kehi Shrine]] in {{ill|Tsuruga, Fukui|en|Tsuruga, Fukui|WD=Q847581|lt=Tsuruga, Fukui}} was lost during the air raids of 1945.{{Efn|Koike thought it looked like an old man riding a peach like a boat, and that it could not be conclusively connected to Momotarō.}}{{sfnp|Koike|1967|pp=36–37}} ====Momotarō's age==== [[File:Momotarō ehon.jpg|thumb|right|360px|Momotaro swinging the magic mallet ({{ill|Uchide no kozuchi|en|Uchide no kozuchi|WD=Q7876713|lt=Uchide no kozuchi}}), with his animal companions.{{right|{{small|―Santō-an Kyōden ({{ill|Santō Kyōden|en|Santō Kyōden|WD=Q938347|lt=Santō Kyōden}}). ''Ehon takara no nanakusa'' (1804)}}}}]] It was noted that the protagonist Momotarō was being drawn progressively younger by artists over the years. In one subjective estimation, Momotarō appeared about age 30-ish until c. 1735, 25-ish up to c. 1800, and 20-ish until the end of Edo Period in 1867.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}} Not every text specifies age, but in the version in {{nihongo|Kamo no Norikiyo|賀茂規清}} (1798–1861)'s {{nihongo|''Hina no Ukegi''|雛迺宇計木}} Momotarō's was 15 years and 6 months when he set out on his expedition.{{sfnp|Koike|1957|p=9}}{{Efn|[[East Asian age reckoning]] applies, so it really means June in the year he turned or will turn 15.}} And in ''Momotarō takara no kurairi'' (c. 1830–40), Momotarō was aged sixteen.{{cite book|author=Ifuku Sanjin |others=Utagawa Hiroshige, illustr. |script-title=ja:桃太郎宝蔵入 |title=Momotarō takara no kurairi |publisher=Sanoya |date=1830–1840|language=ja}}{{cite web|title=Momotaro and the Ogres' Treasure House |work=Edo Picture Books and Japanisme |publisher=National Diet Library |year=2018 |url=https://www.kodomo.go.jp/gallery/edoehon/momotarou/index_e.html |access-date=2019-04-26}} The Momotarō in Iwaya Sazanami's version of 1894 was of similar age (15 years old) when he resolved to go to devil island.{{harvp|Ozaki|1903|p=249}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1904|p=6}}, {{harvp|Iwaya|1927|p=6}}{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The Momotarō illustrated in this work appeared 18 or 19 years old to Koike.{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=38–39}}}} Researcher {{interlanguage link|Namekawa Michio|ja|滑川道夫}} also noticed the trend of Momotarō being depicted younger and younger, and he dubbed the phenomenon {{Nihongo|"tendency of age diminishment"|低年齢化傾向|teinenreika keikō}}.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=99}}{{r|ito}} ===Meiji period=== After Japan abandoned the feudal system and entered the {{ill|Meiji era|en|Meiji era|WD=Q3125096|lt=Meiji era}}, {{interlanguage link|Iwaya Sazanami|ja|巌谷小波}} became a seminal figure in how the Momotaro story was shaped and became familiarized to the Japanese populace. Sazanami was the author of the Momotaro tales in his commercially successful folktale collections, and also a major contributor to the textbook versions. The "Momotarō" tale was first incorporated into nationalized textbooks for [[:en:Elementary schools|Elementary schools]] by the Meiji government in 1887.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{Refn|{{harvp|Torigoe|1983|p=3}}, cited by Hori in English.}}{{harvp|Namekawa|1981|p=ii}}, cited by {{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}} in English. It was subsequently omitted from the 1st edition of the National Language Reader or {{interlanguage link|Kokugo tokuhon{{!}}''Kokugo tokuhon''|ja|国語読本}} but reappeared from the 2nd edition onward to the 5th edition.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}} It has been generally accepted that the 2nd edition reader of 1910 was ''de facto'' written by storybook author Iwaya Sazanami, who had joined the {{ill|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|en|Ministry of Education, Science, Sports and Culture|WD=Q11080185|lt=Ministry of Education}} as nonpermanent staff in 1906.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}{{r|rogala}} Iwaya had already published a version of "Momotaro" (1894) for his ''Nihon mukashibanashi'' ([[:en:Japanese Folktales|Japanese Folktales]]), where Momotaro is cast as a military soldier or commander ({{ill|Shogun|en|Shogun|WD=Q131767|lt=Shogun}}) of Great Japan (Dainihon), dispatched on a punitive campaign to quell the ogres who live in the northeast.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=47}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=66|}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}} Older texts took the punishing of ''oni'' for granted and dispensed with explaining what crimes the oni committed to deserve condemnation. But in Iwaya's version, the ogres were explicitly stated as being evil beings, who devoured the "poor people" and taken "plunder" from the Emperor's land of Japan ({{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Ozaki}}'s translation{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=250}}), thus morally justifying Momotaro's expedition.{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=109}}{{sfnp|Koike|1972|pp=28–29}} It has been suggested these ogres represented the {{ill|Qing dynasty|en|Qing dynasty|WD=Q8733|lt=Qing dynasty}} of China since the publication occurred in 1895, which saw the outbreak of the {{ill|First Sino-Japanese War|en|First Sino-Japanese War|WD=Q178687|lt=Sino-Japanese War}}.{{harvp|Tierney|2005|pp=118, 263}} ===Taishō and Shōwa eras=== From the 3rd edition National Language Reader (1918–1932) onwards (until the end of {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}}), "Momotaro" has occupied the spot of the last tale in Book 1 of these nationalized elementary textbook series.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=55}} Teachers in essays submitted in 1917 stated that the perception of the Momotaro tale was shifting, so that they were seen as containing lessons of assertiveness and helping in the material advancement of one's country.{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Maruyama (1917), p. 17 and Kinoshita (1917), p. 127 There was criticism from the {{ill|Liberalism|en|Liberalism|WD=Q6216|lt=Liberalism}} side, for example, the novelist [[:en:Yuzo Yamamoto|Yamamoto Yūzō]] (1925) protesting that the ''oni'' were being punished for no apparent reason, and is "tantamount to telling [children] to think of foreigners as ''oni''".{{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=55}}, citing Yamamoto (1977), collected works, vol. 10, pp. 288ff In the early {{ill|Shōwa era|en|Shōwa era|WD=Q327567|lt=Shōwa era}}, after Emperor {{ill|Hirohito|en|Hirohito|WD=Q34479|lt=Hirohito}} assumed the throne, Momotarō continued to be used to instill patriotism (or the teachings of the [[Imperial Rescript on Education|Rescript on Education]]) pupils with the 4th edition National Language Reader (1933–1938) which begins with the picture of the cherry blossom.{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=161–162, 179}} The "Momotarō" of the 4th edition was modified so that the ''oni'' now stated "We will no longer torment the people nor take things. Please spare our lives", and forfeits their treasures out of their own volition, thus addressing the foregoing issues (i.e., Momotarō accused of attacking ''oni'' for no legitimate reason).{{harvp|Kahara|2010|pp=51}} and English abstract. The use of Momotarō in wartime propaganda against the U.S. and its Allies was discussed extensively by {{ill|John W. Dower|en|John W. Dower|WD=Q903632|lt=John W. Dower}} in his book ''{{ill|War Without Mercy|en|War Without Mercy|WD=Q55637403|lt=War Without Mercy}}'' (1986). Dower is credited with coining the term "Momotarō paradigm" in this respect.{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|pp=}}{{sfnp|Antoni|1991|pp=165–167}} Momotarō disappeared from Japanese textbooks at the end of World War II.{{harvp|Reider|2010|p=108}}, note 4. ==Oral variants== The story has some regional variations in oral telling. In some variants, a red and white box are seen floating down the river, and when the red box is chosen to be recovered, Momotarō is found inside. These may be a red box and a black box, or the box may contain a peach inside. These types are often seen in the northern parts of Japan ([[:en:Tōhoku|Tōhoku]] and {{ill|Hokuriku region|en|Hokuriku region|WD=Q381025|lt=Hokuriku}} regions).{{sfnp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Seki|1978|pp=81–83}} Or Momotarō may exhibit the characteristic of the lazy protagonist in the {{interlanguage link|Sannen Netarō{{!}}''Netarō''|ja|三年寝太郎}} "Sleeping Boy" stories. These subtypes have been collected mainly in the [[Shikoku]] and {{ill|Chūgoku region|en|Chūgoku region|WD=Q127864|lt=Chūgoku}} regions.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|p=40}}, {{harvp|Kahara|2010|p=53}}{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=334}} There are variances about the Momotarō's process of growth; one is that he grew up to meet the expectation of the old couple to be a fine boy. Another is that he grew up to be a strong but lazy person who just sleeps all day and does not do anything. It is possible that the Momotarō being a fine boy version is more famous to give lessons to children. Nowadays, Momotarō is one of the most famous characters in Japan, as an ideal model for young kids for his kind-heartedness, bravery, power, and care for his parents. Grown up, Momotarō goes on his journey to defeat the demons when he hears about the demons of the Onigashima (demon island). In some versions of the story, Momotarō volunteered to go help the people by repelling the demons, but in some stories he was forced by the townspeople or others to go on a journey. However, all the stories describe Momotarō defeating the Oni and living 'happily ever after' with the old couple. ==Claims as local hero== Momotarō now enjoys popular association with {{ill|Okayama|en|Okayama|WD=Q200078|lt=Okayama}} City or its prefecture, but this association was only created in the modern era.{{harvp|Kahara|2004|pp=51, 61}}, and passim. The publication of a book by Nanba Kinnosuke entitled ''Momotarō no Shijitsu'' (1930) for example helped the notion of Momotarō's origins in Okayama to gain wider familiarity.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|pp=44–47}} Still, even as late as the antebellum period before {{ill|Pacific War|en|Pacific War|WD=Q184425|lt=Pacific War}} (1941–1945), Okayama was considered only the third contender behind two other regions known as Momotarō's homeland.{{sfnp|Kahara|2004|p=51}} The demon island ({{Nihongo|Onigashima|鬼ヶ島}}) of the story is sometimes associated with {{ill|Megijima|en|Megijima|WD=Q339004|lt=Megijima}} Island, an island in the [[Seto Inland Sea]] near {{ill|Takamatsu|en|Takamatsu|WD=Q200707|lt=Takamatsu}}, due to the vast manmade caves found there.{{cite web |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080110004627/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/kankou/B1e.html |archive-date=2008-01-10 |title=Oni-ga-shima(or Megijima) |access-date=2010-09-01}}{{Cite web |title=Megi-jima/Ogi-jima |url=http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |website=Takamatsu City Web Site |access-date=2010-09-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100731105152/http://www.city.takamatsu.kagawa.jp/english/sightseeing/spot/megi-jimaogi-jima.html |archive-date=2010-07-31 |url-status=dead }} {{ill|Inuyama, Aichi|en|Inuyama, Aichi|WD=Q503411|lt=Inuyama, Aichi}} has {{interlanguage link|Momotarō Shrine (Inuyama)|ja|桃太郎神社 (犬山市)|lt=Momotarō Shrine}} with a legend associated with it.{{sfnp|Namekawa|1981|p=42, 461}} In the 1920s and 1930s, lyricist {{ill|Ujō Noguchi|en|Ujō Noguchi|WD=Q2748367|lt=Ujō Noguchi}} wrote three "folk songs" for the locality alluding to the Momotaro legend.{{efn|{{nihongo|《犬山音頭》《桃太郎音頭》《犬山節》|"Inuyama ondo", "Momotarō ondo", "Inuyama bushi"}}.}} ==English translations== [[File:Momotaro-Kobunsha-1885-insidecover.jpg|thumb|English ''Momotaro'' published by {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s Kōbunsha (1885, 1st edition)]] The story has been translated into English many times. "The Adventures of Little Peachling" appeared in [[:en:A.B. Mitford|A.B. Mitford]]'s ''{{ill|Tales of Old Japan|en|Tales of Old Japan|WD=Q7679344|lt=Tales of Old Japan}}'' in 1871. {{ill|William Elliot Griffis|en|William Elliot Griffis|WD=Q2066943|lt=William Elliot Griffis}} published a version in 1880, which remained obscure even to researchers, even though English translations in subsequent decades apparently borrowed from Griffis's phraseology and use of idiom, sometimes even copying outright.{{sfnp|Griffis|1880|pp=62–71}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Rev. David Thompson's translation as "Little Peachling" appeared as the first volume of {{ill|Hasegawa Takejirō|en|Hasegawa Takejirō|WD=Q5678771|lt=Hasegawa Takejirō}}'s ''Japanese Fairy Tale'' series in 1885. A second edition appeared in 1886, with a different set of illustrations, drawn by {{ill|Kobayashi Eitaku|en|Kobayashi Eitaku|WD=Q2784105|lt=Kobayashi Eitaku}} Susan Ballard included the tale in ''Fairy Tales from Far Japan'' (1899). {{ill|Yei Theodora Ozaki|en|Yei Theodora Ozaki|WD=Q8051334|lt=Yei Theodora Ozaki}} included a loosely translated version in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'' (1903); Ozaki's retellings were based on a version by "Sadanami sanjin" (''sic.'', i.e., {{interlanguage link|Sazanami Iwaya|ja|巌谷小波}}).{{harvp|Herring|1988|p=100}}: "..»Sadanami«. This name is a misprint of the ''nom de plume'' of Sazanami Iwaya".{{sfnp|Ozaki|1903|p=v}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} Ozaki was credited with spreading Japanese folktales to the English-speaking nations by researchers such as {{interlanguage link|Teiji Seta|ja|瀬田貞二}}.{{Efn|Seta is well-known as the Japanese translator of [[J. R. R. Tolkien]] novels.}}{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}} There was another English translation that used the same source as Ozaki and published around the same time, namely, "The Story of Peach-Boy" in ''Iwaya's Fairy Tales of Old Japan'' (1903, repub. 1914) translated by {{ill|Hannah Riddell|en|Hannah Riddell|WD=Q5648947|lt=Hannah Riddell}}.{{Refn|group="lower-alpha"|The bilingual 1903 edition was published by Eigaku-shimpo-sha, in 12 volumes. In 1914, the English translations were bound together as "12 parts in 1 vol".}} The translation of the collection was a collaborative effort with other translators, such as Fanny B. Greene, {{ill|Tsuda Umeko|en|Tsuda Umeko|WD=Q514524|lt=Tsuda Umeko}} and others. This latter effort was acknowledged by Iwaya himself.{{harvp|Iwaya|1904}}, foreword.{{sfnp|Herring|1988|p=100}}{{sfnp|Reider|2010|p=240}} Teresa Peirce Williston in her ''Japanese Fairy Tales'', Second Series, in 1911. The tale was translated as ''Peach-Prince and the Demons'' and included in the compilation ''Fairy stories my children love best of all'', although the compiler did not indicate its Japanese origin.Shimer, Edgar Dubs. ''Fairy stories my children love best of all''. New York: L. A. Noble. 1920. pp. 73-79. Momotarō. | first_major = | first_minor = | first_date = | first = | last_major = | last_minor = | last_date = | last = | creator = | based_on = | adapted_by = | designer = | portrayer = | voice = |
